title: Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala — Basic Structure Doctrine
description: The Supreme Court held that Parliament’s power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 is wide but not unlimited. While constitutional amendments may modify or alter provisions including fundamental rights, they cannot destroy or damage the basic structure of the Constitution. Fundamental features such as the supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form of government, secularism, separation of powers, and judicial review form part of this basic structure. The Court upheld the validity of the 24th Amendment affirming Parliament’s amending power, but held that amendments remain subject to the limitation that the essential framework of the Constitution cannot be abrogated.

title: Shafin Jahan v Asokan — Right of Adult to Choose Life Partner
description: The Supreme Court held that a High Court exercising habeas corpus jurisdiction under Article 226 cannot annul the marriage of two consenting adults. The writ of habeas corpus is limited to examining unlawful detention and cannot be used to invalidate personal decisions of competent adults. The Court emphasised that an adult woman has a fundamental right under Articles 19 and 21 to choose her faith and life partner. Parental concern, societal pressure, or ideological objections cannot override individual autonomy and dignity. The doctrine of parens patriae cannot be invoked to control the choices of a competent adult.

title: Union of India v K.A. Najeeb — Bail despite UAPA restrictions
description: The Supreme Court held that constitutional courts may grant bail in cases under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act even though Section 43-D(5) creates stringent restrictions on bail. The Court recognised that prolonged incarceration of undertrial prisoners without the likelihood of an early trial violates the fundamental right to personal liberty under Article 21. Where the accused has spent substantial time in custody and the trial is unlikely to conclude within a reasonable period, the statutory embargo on bail may be relaxed. The Court therefore upheld the High Court’s decision granting bail to the accused.

title: Kunhayammed v State of Kerala — Doctrine of Merger
description: The Supreme Court clarified the doctrine of merger in relation to dismissal of special leave petitions under Article 136. The Court held that when an SLP is dismissed without granting leave, the Supreme Court is not exercising appellate jurisdiction and therefore the judgment of the High Court does not merge into the Supreme Court order. Such dismissal merely indicates that the Court declined to exercise discretionary jurisdiction. Consequently, review of the High Court judgment remains maintainable before the High Court unless leave to appeal has been granted and the Supreme Court has exercised appellate jurisdiction.

title: Indian Young Lawyers Association v State of Kerala — Sabarimala Case
description: The Supreme Court held that the exclusion of women aged 10–50 years from entry into the Sabarimala Temple was unconstitutional. The Court ruled that the practice was discriminatory and violated the principles of equality under Articles 14 and 15, as well as the dignity and autonomy of women protected under Article 21. The Court further held that the devotees of Lord Ayyappa did not constitute a separate religious denomination entitled to exclude women, and that the practice was not an essential religious practice protected under Articles 25 and 26. Rule 3(b) of the Kerala Hindu Places of Public Worship Rules allowing such exclusion was declared unconstitutional.

title: Validity of caste certificate challenge in election petition
description: The Supreme Court held that an election petition challenging the validity of a returned candidate’s caste status must meet a strict evidentiary standard because election disputes are quasi-criminal in nature. The burden of proof lies on the election petitioner and allegations affecting electoral eligibility must be proved beyond reasonable doubt. The Court further clarified that the validity of a caste or community certificate issued by a competent authority cannot be adjudicated collaterally within an election petition. Such certificates can only be challenged before designated statutory scrutiny authorities under the relevant verification laws. Additionally, mere participation in rituals of another religion does not automatically result in loss of Scheduled Caste status unless there is clear, voluntary, and public profession of conversion.
statutes: Representation of the People Act 1951 Section 100

title: Right of an adult to choose a life partner (Hadiya case)
description: The Supreme Court ruled that the High Court exceeded its jurisdiction under Article 226 while exercising habeas corpus powers by annulling the marriage of two consenting adults. The writ of habeas corpus is limited to examining unlawful detention and cannot be used to adjudicate the validity of a marriage once the alleged detainee appears before the court and confirms that she is acting voluntarily. The Court emphasised that a competent adult has a fundamental right under Articles 19 and 21 of the Constitution to choose a life partner and adopt a faith. Parental concern or societal values cannot override an adult individual’s autonomy and dignity. The doctrine of parens patriae is inapplicable to a major person capable of making her own decisions.

title: Sabarimala temple entry and gender equality
description: The Supreme Court held that the exclusion of women aged between 10 and 50 years from entry into the Sabarimala temple violated constitutional guarantees of equality, dignity, and freedom of religion. The practice was based on notions of purity and pollution and was found inconsistent with Articles 14, 15, and 21 of the Constitution. The Court further held that devotees of Lord Ayyappa do not constitute a separate religious denomination entitled to protection under Article 26. Even if denominational rights were assumed, they remain subject to constitutional morality and the reform provisions of Article 25(2)(b). Rule 3(b) of the Kerala Hindu Places of Public Worship Rules allowing exclusion based on custom was declared ultra vires and unconstitutional.
statutes: Kerala Hindu Places of Public Worship Act 1965
Kerala Hindu Places of Public Worship Rules Rule 3(b)

citation: 2024 SC (K. Cheriya Koya v Mohammed Nazer)
title: Requirement of complete record before passing judicial directions
description: The Supreme Court held that when a High Court requisitions the full trial court record for adjudication, it must examine the record before issuing orders affecting the rights or service status of a judicial officer. Passing adverse judicial or disciplinary directions without considering the complete record amounts to adjudication without relevant material and violates principles of procedural fairness. The Court further ruled that disciplinary proceedings initiated solely on the basis of such procedurally defective judicial orders cannot be sustained. Judicial supervision under Article 227 must be exercised with fairness and based on proper consideration of the entire record.

title: Reference to Constitution Bench for interpretation of Article 233
description: The Supreme Court held that questions involving substantial interpretation of Article 233 of the Constitution relating to eligibility for appointment as District Judge raise significant constitutional issues. Article 145(3) mandates that such questions must be decided by a Constitution Bench consisting of at least five judges. Since the cases raised unresolved interpretative issues concerning eligibility of candidates for direct recruitment to the post of District Judge from the Bar, the Court directed that the matter be referred to a Constitution Bench for authoritative determination.

title: Scope of High Court power in second appeal under Section 100 CPC
description: The Supreme Court held that the High Court cannot frame and decide a new substantial question of law in second appeal without proper pleadings, issues, or evidence forming the foundation of such a question. The proviso to Section 100(5) CPC allows framing of an additional substantial question only in exceptional circumstances and with recorded reasons, and the question must arise from the pleadings and findings of the lower courts. The Court ruled that invoking Section 67 of the Indian Succession Act at the stage of second appeal, without it being pleaded or contested during trial, amounted to creating an entirely new case and violated principles of natural justice. Accordingly, the High Court’s judgment was set aside and the validity of the will was restored.

title: Judicial limits on police verification in school administration
description: The Supreme Court held that staff fixation and verification of student strength in aided schools must follow the procedures prescribed under the Kerala Education Act and Rules. The High Court exceeded its jurisdiction by directing police authorities to conduct statewide verification of student enrolment in schools. Such intervention was not contemplated under the statutory framework and risked disrupting academic administration. While the Court acknowledged the need to curb bogus admissions and financial irregularities affecting the public exchequer, it emphasized that corrective mechanisms must be implemented through administrative reforms within the education department rather than through general police involvement.

title: Grant of bail in UAPA cases due to prolonged incarceration
description: The Supreme Court held that statutory restrictions on bail under Section 43-D(5) of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act do not completely bar constitutional courts from granting bail where prolonged pre-trial detention violates the fundamental right to personal liberty under Article 21. Although the statute imposes a stringent threshold for bail in terrorism-related offences, the Court clarified that the rigour of such provisions may be relaxed where the accused has been incarcerated for a long period and the trial is unlikely to conclude within a reasonable time. In such circumstances, constitutional courts are empowered to grant bail to safeguard the right to a speedy trial and personal liberty.

title: Directory vs mandatory interpretation of procedural rules
description: The Supreme Court held that Rule 22 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules prescribing the quantity of food sample for analysis is directory rather than mandatory. The Court explained that the use of the word 'shall' in statutory language is not determinative of mandatory intent and must be interpreted in light of legislative purpose. If the quantity of sample sent to the Public Analyst, though less than prescribed, is sufficient to enable reliable analysis, the evidentiary value of the report remains valid and the prosecution is not vitiated. Only where the deficiency prevents accurate analysis would the trial be affected. The Court clarified and overruled earlier precedent that treated non-compliance as automatically fatal.
statutes: Prevention of Food Adulteration Act 1954 Section 11
Prevention of Food Adulteration Act 1954 Section 16
Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules 1955 Rule 22

title: Circumstantial evidence and commutation of death sentence
description: The Supreme Court upheld the conviction of the accused for multiple murders and rape based entirely on circumstantial evidence, including motive, last seen theory, recovery of bodies, false explanations, and corroborative forensic and DNA evidence. The Court reiterated that a conviction can be sustained where the chain of circumstantial evidence is complete and points unerringly to the guilt of the accused. However, while affirming the conviction under Sections 302, 376, and 201 IPC, the Court commuted the death sentence to life imprisonment after considering mitigating circumstances such as absence of prior criminal history, long incarceration, and evidence suggesting the possibility of reformation. The case reaffirmed the application of the 'rarest of rare' doctrine in capital sentencing.
statutes: Code of Criminal Procedure Sections 366 and 368

title: Promotion eligibility and interpretation of executive recruitment orders
description: The Supreme Court held that where statutory recruitment rules are absent, appointments and promotions in public service may be governed by executive orders issued under the authority of Article 309 of the Constitution. In this case, the Government Order regulating appointments in the Medical Education Service did not require that the stipulated years of teaching experience be acquired after obtaining the postgraduate qualification. The High Court erred by reading such a requirement into the executive order. The Court emphasized that where the executive rule expressly includes a requirement in one context but omits it in another, the omission must be treated as deliberate (expressio unius est exclusio alterius). Consequently, the High Court’s interpretation was set aside and the tribunal’s decision was restored.
statutes: Kerala State and Subordinate Services Rules Rule 10(ab)
Kerala State and Subordinate Services Rules Rule 28(b)

title: Judicial review of compromise decrees obtained through fraud
description: The Supreme Court held that a compromise decree entered into by a statutory authority can be challenged in writ proceedings where allegations of fraud or collusion are made. The statutory bar under Order 23 Rule 3A of the Code of Civil Procedure, which prohibits filing a separate suit to set aside a compromise decree, does not prevent constitutional courts from examining such decrees where public interest or trust property is involved. The Court emphasized that statutory authorities managing temple or public trust properties act in a fiduciary capacity and cannot compromise or alienate such property in violation of prior judicial directions. Any settlement that defeats earlier court orders or results in unlawful transfer of trust property is liable to be set aside.
statutes: Code of Civil Procedure Order 23 Rule 3A

title: Interpretation of ceiling provisions under Kerala Land Reforms Act
description: The Supreme Court clarified the operation of ceiling provisions under the Kerala Land Reforms Act in relation to conversion of land and retrospective invalidation of transfers. The Court held that Section 82(4) must be interpreted as taking effect from the date the provision came into force rather than the original enactment date of the statute. It further held that a purchase certificate issued under Section 72K is conclusive only with respect to assignment of tenancy rights and does not bind the Taluk Land Board in determining surplus land under ceiling proceedings. Additionally, Section 84(3) was interpreted as having retrospective operation, thereby invalidating certain transfers made after the specified statutory date.

title: Legislative competence to impose building tax
description: The Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of the Kerala Building Tax Act, 1975, holding that the State Legislature possessed competence under Entry 49 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to impose taxes on buildings. The Court clarified the distinction between the subject of a tax and the measure used to compute it, observing that determining capital value by multiplying annual rental value was a permissible method of valuation. The retrospective operation of the tax from an earlier date was also upheld, as it did not violate constitutional protections or impair vested rights. The Court rejected the challenge under Article 14, finding the valuation mechanism reasonable and non-arbitrary.
statutes: Constitution of India Entry 49 List II
